source.title: Probing Out-of-Distribution Robustness of Language Models with Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning
source.authors: Hyunsoo Cho; Choonghyun Park; Junyeob Kim; Hyuhng Joon Kim; Kang Min Yoo; Sang-goo Lee

record.tranche_reason: It tests how OOD detection performance changes across language-model scales, a different outcome from pretraining loss but relevant to the downstream-performance version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The study measures OOD detection performance as model scale changes, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find a compute-optimal allocation. Its numeric AUROC tables compare models and evaluation or transfer settings; the text's stated scale trends are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The study measures OOD-detection AUROC across six autoregressive LMs of increasing size (GPT2-S to GPT-J). This is a downstream-task result bearing on V6 in a new setting. It fits no scaling law and reports no pretraining loss, so it speaks only to whether performance rises with scale, not to how predictably.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that model scale is an important factor in OOD robustness, mostly for far-OOD, while close-OOD stays hard. Frozen large models still lag far behind fine-tuned BERT-base. PETL methods beat fine-tuning on sufficiently large PLMs. Last-token representation-based OOD scoring transfers poorly to autoregressive models.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates OOD detection across model scales and transfer methods; it does not use or reproduce a power-law loss-fitting recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scale trend differs by OOD setting: far-OOD performance improves with scale, while close-OOD improvement is limited and saturates.
record.problems: The study reports OOD detection metrics, not held-out pretraining loss or fitted scaling laws. The scale-trend descriptions are qualitative, and the model parameter counts are not stated in the results.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's numeric AUROC tables (Tables 1 and 2) report results across backbones, evaluation methods, and transfer settings, but do not report pretraining loss or fitted/predicted scaling laws; the qualitative scale findings relevant to V6 are captured in r1–r2.

untested.parts: Fitting a predictive curve of downstream performance against scale or pretraining loss; extrapolation to larger models; any relation to pretraining loss.

missing.what: Linear-probe (SLP) AUROC by backbone. Far-OOD: 83.03, 87.39, 88.47, 89.55, 89.44, 91.94. Close-OOD: 72.97, 75.17, 80.46, 77.59, 86.55, 89.12. Both show non-monotonic steps.
Fine-tuning and PETL AUROC by backbone, including the GPT-Neo prefix-tuning collapse (90.25/89.81/88.98 far-OOD; 81.9/80.82 close-OOD) and GPT-Neo falling below GPT2-XL under fine-tuning.
LoRA AUROC by backbone and evaluation method. Mahalanobis and cosine scores jump from about 77–82 (GPT2-S/M) to about 97 (GPT2-L), a step rather than a smooth trend.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V6: there are only six models, parameter counts are unstated, and the study fits no curve. The scale ordering is confounded because GPT-Neo and GPT-J differ in training data from GPT2. Figure 2's caption duplicates Figure 1's ('without updating'), although Figure 2 shows tuned methods.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from smaller-run fits.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effect of architecture details at fixed parameter count on loss.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests OOD detection performance across model scales, not performance on a broad range of downstream tasks or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: GPT2-S, GPT2-M, GPT2-L, GPT2-XL, GPT-Neo, and GPT-J (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Different scales; numeric parameter counts not stated for these models in the results.
rows.stage_stated: Frozen pretrained models; no parameter tuning
rows.operation_detail: Compared OOD detection performance across model scales without tuning model parameters.
rows.value: The authors report that performance improves as model size increases; they describe far-OOD detection capability as improving proportionally with size.
rows.note: Qualitative trend stated in the text; the figure's underlying values are not transcribed numerically here.
rows.check: The frozen-model trend comes from Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 1(a), which give no numeric values. The 'improves proportionally' wording is from Sec. 3.3, which discusses tuned models, not frozen ones. Parameter counts are never stated, and GPT-Neo's size variant is unspecified.

rows.size_stated: Different scales; numeric parameter counts not stated for these models in the results.
rows.stage_stated: Frozen pretrained models; no parameter tuning
rows.operation_detail: Compared OOD detection performance across model scales without tuning model parameters.
rows.value: The authors report that improvement with scale saturates in the close-OOD setting and is comparatively trivial.
rows.note: The paper says this setting remains challenging and that a gap from the fine-tuned small model remains.
rows.check: The state is right per the text ('saturates', 'improves rather trivially'). The value is qualitative only; Table 2 linear-SLP close-OOD numbers, not recorded, show a larger rise from 72.97 to 89.12.

relationships.condition: Far-OOD (CLINC), frozen models and most tuned settings
relationships.reason: Authors report OOD detection improves with model size (r1). Table 2 SLP far-OOD AUROC rises from 83.03 (GPT2-S) to 91.94 (GPT-J); this number is from the text, not a row.
relationships.display_finding: Detection improved with model size, with SLP far-out-of-distribution AUROC increasing from 83.03 for GPT2-S to 91.94 for GPT-J.

relationships.condition: Close-OOD (Banking split) and specific backbone/method combinations
relationships.reason: Gains saturate in close-OOD (r2). Per Tables 1–2 (text, not rows), the trend is non-monotonic: GPT-Neo falls below GPT2-XL, and prefix-tuning on GPT-Neo drops to about 81–90. Mahalanobis and cosine jump stepwise from GPT2-M to GPT2-L.
relationships.display_finding: Close-OOD gains saturated, GPT-Neo underperformed GPT2-XL and dropped to about 81–90 with prefix tuning, while Mahalanobis and cosine methods jumped from GPT2-M to GPT2-L.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
